note: What the province remembers from before the Empire, and what is believed about it. `The Stone Nests` is a three-volume series (RI-LOR03 §2, ≥3 series) holding position A of CF-D003 — the antiquarian's view that the natives inherited ruins they could not have built — which The Egg Speaks Twice denies in its Seventh Song and which nothing in the game adjudicates; per RI-LOR06, position A is a wrong view held sincerely by real people and a critic must not flag it as an error. Three texts here are declared evidence for sealed mysteries in corpus/50-world/sealed/SEALED-ANSWERS.md (M-01, M-02, M-03) and were named there before they existed; each is written to under-determine its answer and none contains a declared leak n-gram. The last two are the pair mainline.json UA-02 relies on: two incompatible accounts of the same building, neither corroborated.

books.title: The Stone Nests of Argonia, Volume the First: A Survey of Eleven Sites
books.author: Serjo Fals Rethan, of Mournhold, sometime Antiquary to the Provincial Office
books.unreliability: Careful, well-measured, and it is the measuring that makes the next volume possible. He is a good surveyor and a bad thinker and the first volume only shows the first half of that.
books.text:
I have visited eleven of the stone nests of this province in four seasons and I have measured each of them with the same rod, which is more than any author before me can claim, and I say so at the outset because it is the only claim in this volume I expect to survive.

The form is constant and it is worth stating plainly for a reader who has only seen the woodcuts. A stone nest is a stepped mass, square at the base, rising in terraces that diminish by a fixed proportion, and the proportion is the same at every site I have measured: each terrace is seven parts in nine of the one below it. Not approximately. At Ix-Thakla, where the base course is intact for its whole run, I measured a hundred and forty paces on the lowest terrace and a hundred and nine on the second, and if the reader will do the arithmetic he will find that a builder who wanted a pleasing shape and did it by eye does not land on that twice, let alone eleven times across four hundred miles of swamp.

The terraces are joined by causeways, and the causeways are the second constant. They run between sites and not toward them; that is, a causeway leaves the third terrace of one nest and arrives at the third terrace of another, and takes no notice whatever of the ground between, which in five of the eleven cases is standing water. Where the water is deep the causeway is carried on piers. Where the water is very deep the causeway simply goes into it and comes out on the far side, and I have had a native pole me along one for half a mile with the stones a fathom under the hull, perfectly true, laid on a bottom no one has looked at since they were laid.

The stone. This is where I depart from the received account and I ask the reader's patience because it is the only place in this volume where I depart from anything. It is said, and repeated, and repeated again, that the nests are built of local stone. They are not. At Ix-Thakla, at Sunken Teeth, and at the drowned one south of Helstrom, the facing courses are a hard pale limestone that does not occur within eighty miles of any of the three. I have carried samples. I have set them against the quarry faces of the Salt Hills and they do not match, and I have set them against a piece brought from the Nibenay and the reader may draw his own conclusion, which I decline to draw for him in a volume of measurements.

On the interiors I can say almost nothing and I will not pretend otherwise. Nine of the eleven are solid, or filled, or filled and then solid; there is no chamber, no shaft, no stair. Of the remaining two, one is under water at every hour I attended it, and one has a doorway on the fourth terrace which the rootkeepers of that district would not let me approach, and I did not force the matter, having been told by a man of the Cohorts that the wrong sort of insistence in this province is a way of being found later.

I record what I was told at each site by whoever would speak to me, without comment, because comment belongs in the second volume.

At Ix-Thakla: that their grandmothers built it. At Sunken Teeth: that their grandmothers built it. At the drowned one: that their grandmothers built it, and that it was built twice, and that the second time it was built lower. At Nine-Mud, where there is no nest but there is a causeway going into the marsh from nothing at all: that it goes to a nest, and that the nest is there, and that it is simply not up any more.

Eleven sites. Four seasons. One rod. The reader who wants a theory is directed to the second volume, which he will enjoy more and should trust less.

books.title: The Stone Nests of Argonia, Volume the Second: On Their Authorship
books.author: Serjo Fals Rethan, of Mournhold
books.unreliability: Wrong, and wrongly for a reason that is not about stones. He has decided in advance what the people he is describing are capable of, and every measurement in the first volume is then bent to fit it.
books.text:
In the first volume I measured. In this one I shall reason, and I am aware that reasoning is the part a man is remembered for being wrong about.

The question is simple to state. Somebody built eleven stepped masses of dressed limestone, to a fixed proportion, joined by causeways laid on the beds of drowned rivers, in a country with no roads, no wheeled carriage, no draught animal that will work in water, and no quarry within eighty miles of three of the sites. Who?

The natives say: our grandmothers. They say it uniformly and they say it without heat, in the tone a farmer uses about a wall. I have heard it at every site and I record it faithfully and I do not believe it, and I shall set out why, and I shall do it without the sneering that has disfigured this subject since Vabdas.

First. A people who build in dressed stone go on building in dressed stone. It is the most persistent habit a civilisation has; it outlasts its gods. The Saxhleel of today build in reed, in stilt, in mud brick where the ground allows and in nothing at all where it does not. There is not one dressed course laid by an Argonian hand in living memory, nor in the memory of the Cohorts, nor in any document of the Office. A skill is not mislaid the way a coin is mislaid. It goes out over generations and leaves a trail of worse and worse work behind it, and there is no trail. There is high work, and then there is reed.

Second. The proportion. Seven in nine, at eleven sites, over four hundred miles. That is not a tradition; that is a specification. A specification implies a body that issues it and a body that enforces it, and enforcement implies a state, and a state leaves a great deal more behind it than eleven buildings. It leaves boundary stones, tax marks, standard measures, a written hand. This province has none of these things and never has had. What it has is eleven perfect buildings sitting in a country that shows no other sign of ever having been organised at all.

Third, and I put it last because it is the one that will be quoted against me. The stone came from outside. Whoever cut those facing courses cut them somewhere else and moved them here, and a people who can move eighty miles of limestone through standing water can also, one presumes, write something down.

My conclusion, offered as a conclusion and not as a fact, is that the stone nests are the work of a builder who is not in this province now and possibly never lived in it, and that the Saxhleel came into a landscape already furnished and did what any sensible people do with a furnished landscape, which is to occupy it and to say that it was always theirs. There is no shame in this. Half of Cyrodiil is Ayleid underneath and we do not blush.

I am told, and I record it because I record everything, that the natives find this suggestion offensive. I have had it explained to me by a keeper at Helstrom, at some length, that I have made an error of a kind she called a rope error, which I understood to mean that I had taken hold of the wrong end of something. She would not elaborate and I did not press her. I would only observe that being offended by a hypothesis is not an argument against it, and that in twenty years of this work I have never once been offered a measurement in reply.

The third volume will treat of the causeways and of the objection, raised by three correspondents, that a country which forgets its builders is a country that has been made to forget.

books.title: The Stone Nests of Argonia, Volume the Third: Replies to My Critics
books.author: Serjo Fals Rethan, of Mournhold, formerly Antiquary to the Provincial Office
books.unreliability: The volume where the argument stops being about stones. He answers the weakest letter at length and the strongest one in a footnote, and he has stopped measuring anything.
books.text:
This volume was not planned. It exists because the second was read.

To the correspondent at Gideon who accuses me of contempt for the Saxhleel: I have spent four seasons in their water and he has spent none, and I invite him to name the passage. He will not, because there is none, and because what he objects to is not contempt but a conclusion he dislikes, and it is a great convenience to a man to be able to call a conclusion a discourtesy.

To the correspondent at Stormhold who observes that the Saxhleel build in reed because reed is what grows and stone is eighty miles away: this is the best of the letters and I shall be brief with it, which the reader may make of what he likes. Yes. The point is fair. It does not touch the proportion.

To Quartermaster Verrent of the Ninth, who writes to me privately and then publishes the letter, which I shall remember: he says that I have never asked a rootkeeper a question I did not already have the answer to. He is a man who counted grain for nineteen years and has lately discovered the soul, and I would gently suggest that a ledger is not a training in inference. He says the natives told me the truth eleven times and I wrote down that they had said it and not that it was so. That is precisely what a record is. If I had wanted to write down what I believed, I should have written a devotional.

And to the several correspondents who ask why, if the nests were built by others, the causeways go from third terrace to third terrace and never to the ground: I do not know, and I said in the first volume that I did not know, and I notice that nobody quotes that.

I shall add one thing, and then I shall stop, because I am sixty-one and this subject has taken more of me than it was worth.

At the drowned nest south of Helstrom, on my last visit, an old keeper let me sit on the second terrace with her for an afternoon, which nobody had done before. She asked me what I thought the building was for. I said that I did not know, and that I doubted her people had built it. She was not offended in the least. She said: you have asked the wrong question twice, and both times you asked it about the stone.

I asked her what the right question was.

She said: ask what it is standing on.

I have thought about this for two years. I take it to be a piece of native indirection of the sort one collects in this country, and I would not report it at all except that I have found I cannot get rid of it. The foundations of every nest I measured are under water or under mud or both, and I did not dig one of them, and I am now too old to go back, and I record here, against my own case, that the whole of my argument rests on eleven buildings whose bottoms I never saw.

The reader will do what he likes with that. I have set down what I measured, what I concluded, and where the hole in it is, which is more than my critics have done, and it will have to serve for a life's work.

books.title: On the Tally-Stones of the Blackwood, with a Note on Their Ornament
books.author: Aurelia Sitte, Surveyor, in the service of the Provincial Office
books.unreliability: Every measurement in it is correct and the conclusion is wrong, and the conclusion is wrong because she decided what the object was before she counted anything on it.
books.wrong_on_purpose: Concludes the obelisk is an Imperial-era boundary marker with a decorative motif. It is not. Nothing in the game corrects her.
books.text:
A short paper, offered to the Office in support of a claim for expenses.

The stone stands in open ground four hours east of Gideon on the Blackwood road, where the trees give out and the ground is firm enough to take a cart. It is a single mass, four-faced, twenty-two feet in the standing part, of the pale hard limestone that occurs in this province only in worked form, on which I have written elsewhere and about which I shall say nothing further here.

It is covered on all four faces with short cut notches. They begin low on the northern face, run in even columns, and continue up and around. I have counted the northern and eastern faces entire and estimated the southern, and I have not counted the western because the last third of it is above the reach of my ladder and I was not going to hire scaffolding for a footnote.

The notches are hand-cut. They are not weathering and they are not tool-marks from the dressing; they are deliberate, of a uniform depth, made with a chisel of about a thumb's width, and they have been made over a very long period by a great many different hands. This is plain from the strokes. The lower courses are cut by someone with a strong wrist and a habit of undercutting to the left. Three or four feet up the habit changes. It changes again, and again, and I counted eleven distinct habits before I stopped counting habits and started counting notches.

Here is the useful part, and it is the only original thing in this paper.

On the eastern face there is a stretch of forty-one notches that fall between two datable events: a course of soot from the Gideon warehouse fire, which the Office's own records place exactly, and a limewash that was applied when the road was surveyed and which I can date from my predecessor's expense claim. Forty-one notches between them, and three hundred and seventy-four days. That is a notch every nine days and a tenth of a day, and I have checked the arithmetic because I did not expect it to come out so evenly.

An even interval is the whole of the matter. Whatever is being cut into this stone is being cut on a schedule, and a schedule implies an office, and an office implies a purpose that somebody was once paid for.

My conclusion is that the stone is a march-marker of the older sort, set to divide two holdings, and that the notches are the ornament proper to that class of monument — a tally of seasons or of tolls, cut by the tenant of the nearer holding as a form of rent-record, in the way that the notched posts of the West Weald record a share of a harvest. The interval of nine days and a fraction is awkward for a season and awkward for a month, but the marsh year is not our year and I would not press the point.

There is at present an old woman who cuts the notches. She was there when I arrived and she was there when I left and she cut four notches in the fortnight I was in the district. I did not interview her. I record, for the sake of completeness, that she was entirely willing to be watched, that she used her own chisel, and that when I asked one of the carters what she was doing he said she was doing what her mother did. This is the ordinary answer in this province and it is not information.

I would recommend the Office no further expenditure on the site. It is a boundary stone with a long-lived local custom attached to it, of the sort that any province produces in quantity, and I have spent eleven days and four ladders establishing that its ornament is regular, which is a modest result honestly come by.

Expenses appended.

books.title: What Was Agreed at the Water: an account by an elder of the Oliis
books.author: unsigned; a Kothringi hand, late in the Flu years
books.unreliability: It breaks off. Everything that would identify the other party to the agreement is in the part that is missing, and the writer plainly assumed the reader would already know.
books.text:
…and it was three years then since the last boat had come up from the coast with anyone alive on it, and I will not write down what we did in the second of those years.

I am setting this out because the young will be told a shorter version, and the shorter version will be that we were saved, and I want it written by somebody who was in the room that the saving was a bargain and that a bargain has two sides.

We did not seek it. That must be first. It came to the water below the town, and it came in the manner of a thing arriving that has been travelling a long time, and it spoke to Ehlta first because Ehlta was at the landing and not for any other reason that I have ever been able to find. She was not chosen. She was standing there.

The terms were put to the elders over four nights. I will set down what I can.

That we would not be taken by the sickness, and that this would hold for all of us and not for some.

That we would not be moved from this ground, ever, by anything.

That what was asked in return would be asked once and would be paid once, and that after the paying nothing further would be asked of us for as long as the town stood.

That the paying could not be undone by us, and — this was Ehlta's question, and she asked it three times, and I am glad she asked it — that it could not be undone by it either.

The elders argued for four nights and there was no honest argument against it except the one Ehlta made, which was that a bargain you cannot read the whole of is not a bargain, it is a hand held out in the dark, and that we should ask it plainly what it was. And we did ask it plainly, on the third night, and it answered plainly, and the answer is the reason there was a fourth night.

Eight households said no on the fourth night. By the following spring there were four households saying no and the four were not the same four.

I have set down elsewhere what the paying was and I am not going to set it down twice.

What I want written here, by me, while I still have the hand for it, is that we were not tricked. Nobody was tricked. It said what it wanted and it said what it would give and it has given exactly what it said, which I know because I am writing this and I should not be. The thing that is wrong with the bargain is not in the terms. It is in what we thought the words meant when we agreed to them, and I have come to think that it knew that, and that knowing it is not the same as lying, and that this is a distinction I would not have accepted from a man and I am accepting from

books.title: Survey of the Ridge Above Tenmarch: sheet four of six
books.author: the Ninth Cohort, survey party under Serjeant Bruccius Vale
books.unreliability: A competent survey of what the party could find. The count is wrong and there is no way for the party to have known that.
books.text:
Sheet four of six. Sheets one to three cover the road and the crossing at Tenmarch and are filed separately. Sheets five and six were not made; the party was recalled.

Item. The ridge carries a number of vertical shafts in the rock, open at the top, of a bore between two and three feet, which the carters call the flutes and which are audible from the road at any hour that there is wind, which is every hour.

Item. Thirteen shafts were found and are marked on the sheet at the paces given. The party walked the ridge twice, once from the Tenmarch end and once from the Archon end, and got thirteen both times. Serjeant Vale notes that the ground is broken and that a fourteenth is not to be ruled out; the party had four days and used them.

Item. The bore is regular. Measured at the mouth on nine of the thirteen: two feet seven, two feet seven, two feet six, two feet seven, two feet seven, two feet seven, two feet seven, two feet six, two feet seven. The four not measured are on the far face and could not be reached without rope the party did not carry.

Item. The spacing is regular. Along the crest the interval is forty-one paces to fifty-two, which is not regular; but taken as a line drawn through the shafts and disregarding the crest, the interval is forty-four paces, eleven times out of twelve.

Item. The sound. Seven notes, and they do not change. The party attended at four hours of the day and in wind from three quarters and the notes were the same seven each time, in the same relation to each other, differing only in loudness. Legionary Ostro, who was a chapel singer at Bruma, has written the seven down on the reverse of this sheet in the notation he was taught, and the party takes no position on whether that notation is any use to the Office.

Item. Depth. A stone dropped down the nearest shaft was not heard to land. A second stone with a cord bent to it was let down to the whole of the cord, which is a hundred and ten feet, without touching. The party did not have more cord. Serjeant Vale declined to send a man down on the grounds that the Office had asked for a survey of the road.

Item. There is a quarryman at Tenmarch who says he has lowered a lamp into one of them and that the lamp went out at a depth he would not put a number to. He was not sober. It is recorded because the Office asks for everything.

Item. No worked stone, no tool-marks at the mouths, no spoil. Whatever made these shafts, if anything made them, did not leave the rock it took out anywhere the party could find in four days.

Signed, Vale, at Tenmarch Bridge.

books.title: Of the House Under the Wastes, Which Was Built in Reverence
books.author: Ojal-Weeth, of the Drowned Court, from an older text he does not name
books.unreliability: A devotional reading of a building nobody has been inside, made from an older text the author will not identify, by a man who wants the answer he gets.
books.answers_unanswered: UA-02 (one of two incompatible accounts; neither is corroborated)

contradicts.on: what the house under the Stone Wastes was built to do

books.text:
There is a house under the Stone Wastes. This is not disputed by anyone who has walked that ground with their boots off. The stone rings hollow from the Bone Ladder to the third salt pan, and it rings in a pattern, and a pattern under your feet is a floor.

What is disputed is what it was for, and I have been asked to set out the reading I was taught, which is the older of the two readings and which the Court has kept without ever committing itself to it.

The house was built in reverence. I will show why.

Everything in this country goes down. That is the first thing a hatchling is told and the last thing an old one says. The water goes down, the dead go down, the roots go down, and below the roots there is no root, and that is not a horror, it is the shape of the world and the shape is not an insult to anybody. A people who understand this do not build a wall against it. You do not wall off the ground.

So: a house is built, on the way down, in the path of everything that is going down, and it is built well. It is built by people who could lay a causeway on a river bed and make it true. It is not a plug and it is not a trap. It is a stop on a road, and what is a stop on a road for?

It is for resting. It is for being received. Consider what our own house does. The Court takes a body at whatever hour, of whatever people, in whatever condition, and asks nothing, and holds it, and gives it over. We do not think we are stealing anyone. We are the last hands, and being the last hands is a courtesy, and we built a house on a stair to do it in.

The older text I was taught from — and I will not name it, because I was taught it under a condition and the condition was that it stayed in the room — describes the house under the Wastes in words that are the same words we use for a mortuary. Not similar words. The same three words, in the same order, and in the older negative. The people who built it thought they were doing what we think we are doing. They built a place for the going-down to be honoured on its way, and then they went away, or Duskfall took them, or both.

I am aware of the other reading and I will state it fairly, because a reading you have to misstate is a reading you have already lost to. The other reading is that the house was built in fear: that the builders understood exactly what is under everything, and did not want it to have what was theirs, and made a vessel to keep it out of. It is not a foolish reading. It accounts for the same floor.

But it requires that a people who built eleven perfect terraces up toward the sky also built one perfect box against the ground, in the same generation, out of the same stone, meaning the opposite thing by it. I have never been able to hold both of those in one hand.

And there is this, which is not an argument. If you go out onto the Wastes at the turn of the tide and stand still and take your boots off, the floor under you is not a frightened thing. I know what I have said. I know exactly how much that is worth. I have written it down anyway, because the other side writes down what they felt out there too, and theirs gets called evidence.

books.title: Of the House Under the Wastes, Which Was Built in Fear
books.author: Undersexton Bel Mourne
books.unreliability: Sharp, evidenced, and built on an analogy she never examines: she is reasoning about a building from the habits of the people who bury in it now, four hundred years and an entire culture downstream of whoever laid the floor.
books.answers_unanswered: UA-02 (one of two incompatible accounts; neither is corroborated)

contradicts.on: what the house under the Stone Wastes was built to do

books.text:
Ojal-Weeth has written that the house under the Wastes was built in reverence, from a text he declines to name, on an argument from the habits of a burial house four hundred years younger than the floor he is describing. I have read it twice. I am going to answer it, and I am going to do it without the word offensive, which is the word that ends every argument in this province.

Start with what is actually out there.

The Wastes ring hollow over a stretch that I have walked and paced at something over two miles on the long axis. Under the third salt pan the ring changes and goes dead, in a line, and the line is straight for as far as I could follow it, which was four hundred paces. A straight dead line in a hollow floor is a wall. Not a partition — a wall thick enough to kill the sound, in a building whose other walls do not.

At the seaward end the hollow stops at a rise that is not a natural rise. It is faced. Under six inches of salt crust there is dressed limestone laid in courses, and the courses are laid to shed water away from the hollow and not toward it. Anybody who has built anything knows what that means. That is not a threshold. Nobody makes a doorway that pushes the visitor away from the door.

And there are the intakes. There are at least six of them and there may be more; they are shafts, they come up through the crust at intervals, they are cut, and every one of them is fitted at the throat with worked stone that narrows the bore. You do not narrow the throat of a thing you are welcoming.

Anybody may go and look at the facing, and I would rather they did than take it from me. You walk out of Soulrest north on the coast track and turn seaward off it at the second withy post, and then it is about a quarter-hour over the crust with the water on your right until the ground stops ringing. The rise is in front of you when it stops. Take your boots off before the third salt pan or you will walk over the whole thing and hear nothing.

Ojal-Weeth says a mortuary. A mortuary is open at one end. A mortuary is a room you carry a body into and out of, and the whole of its design is about getting through it. This is a vessel. It has a lid, it has a wall, it has a wall thick enough to be a decision, and its openings are throttled. If a builder wanted to receive what was coming down, the cheapest possible design is a hole. This is the most expensive possible design, and every expensive part of it is spent on restriction.

Now I will say the part that will get this paper put at the back of the shelf.

We are all very careful in this province to say that going down is not a punishment and not a reward and that the people who made it a punishment came here on ships. I have heard that line since I arrived and I have said it myself. I notice that the people who say it most often are the people whose grandmothers built a two-mile box against it.

I do not think the builders were foreigners and I do not think they had our religion. I think they knew something specific — not a doctrine, a fact — and I think they spent the wealth of a province on a container, and I think the reason nobody can tell us what they knew is that the knowing did not outlast Duskfall and the container did.

Ojal-Weeth ends by saying that if you stand out there with your boots off, the floor is not a frightened thing. I have stood out there with my boots off. I agree with him about what it feels like. I would only observe that a strongbox does not feel frightened either, and that this is not usually taken as evidence about what is inside it.
